en: Now caught with a threatening lasso;
Narkyzyl, whom he would not yield in play,
He hauled away with a mighty jerk.
Before the bloodstained lion
He brought the bounding creature
And offered him as a gift.
Khan Manas's forty companions
Went along side by side;
Ajybay and Bakay, the two khans,
Before the greathearted lion
Brought the creature prancing
And arrived with him.
Do not ask about Bakay:
As long as he lived, his speech was plain;
A judge of horses, a knower of men,
Lion Bakay had second sight.
When he faced an opposing foe,
Your elder, lion Bakay,
Had skill as well;
A matchless finder of counsel,
He also had great prowess.
Before lion Manas,
Leading Narkyzyl,
Speaking softly, weighing his words,
About Narkyzyl's worth
Greathearted Bakay began:
“He does not tire on scouting rides;
This formidable Narkyzyl
Will not fail on a baggage-train march.
Ride him six months—he will not grow lean;
Until his sixtieth tooth-year
He will not age with his teeth worn down.
Unflustered at the battle cry,
He shows exceptional qualities.
In the darkness of the moon
He never puts a single hoof wrong;
The places his hooves touch
Split apart on every side.
Viewed from every angle,
Narbuudan is a marvel,
Showing the marks of a winged steed.
Ride him on a six-month journey:
He will not weaken and leave you caught.
Unless a hand's breadth of rein remains,
He will not let a determined foe seize you.
Whatever you load on him is no burden;
He is a creature wiser than a man,
Only lacking a tongue to speak.
For the creature he would not give when asked
I felt such longing that I made a quarrel.
Zhanaaly is no ally of ours;
I put that bastard to the test.
By leaving Karach mounted,
What purpose shall we achieve?
Now that the horse is in our hands,
Let us take him trotting away.
I have something striking to tell you:
To split lungs and sever heads,
To burst gall and spill blood,
You have many foes, if you count them.
Before you stand the Baran;
You have many peoples to contend with;
On your flank are the Chinese.
Your elder Bakay has this to say:
Should we happen to fight,
Alöökö's son Kongurbay
Has that very vengeance to seek.
You have started much suffering:
The hero Khan Alöökö
You seized and slaughtered.”
Greathearted Bakay said this,
Making him know what he did not know,
And the wolf-maned one touched by Khizir
He thus brought onto the right path.
Manas, touched by Khizir,
Bakay led and made a hero;
He drove white deer and made them cattle,
And all who fought him
He weakened and threw into confusion.
He broke through stone and opened roads,
Maiming those he faced.
He slashed those who assailed him,
Set grassy ground on fire,
Kindled the dry pasture,
Poured blood into clear water.
Dust rose where he marched;
Souls fled at the sound of him.
He broke royal camps and took plunder;
In the days of your mighty warrior
He attacked many lands.
He brought low those he encountered,
Slashed those who clashed with him,
And those who roused his anger
He drove before him.
Those who crossed his will,
In the days of your mighty warrior,
He caught in his jaws and chewed.
Of all that ears heard and eyes saw,
None remained to turn back his lasso.
His fortunes stood complete:
From ill-intentioned Jakyp
Fierce lion Manas arose.
Breaking royal camps, taking gold coins,
The heroes took as plunder
A thousand dark-eyed captives,
Making known that Sultan Manas,
The bloodstained warrior, was a lion.
From the hands of Khan Karach,
Narkyzyl, whom he had demanded,
He gave Akylay to ride.
They slew the enemies they faced,
And gold coins and precious stones
They amassed in plunder.
They spread their prowess beyond measure,
And the two giants, Zhanaaly and Karach,
With the people of Chambyl-Bel, they subdued.
Manas became Manas, they say;
He mounted his horse in grandeur, they say.
Governing the people, ruling the land,
He won the name of Leopard, they say.
Forty mighty men came from forty lands;
His fortunes stood complete.
If you looked into his heart,
It was broader than the face of the earth.
Returning once more to Talas,
The Argyn and Kyrgyz turned toward the plains;
That was when they settled there.
The bloodstained lion, like a blue tick—
That was when he grew full and strong.
They made his worth known to the people,
Placed a golden crown upon him,
Seated him upon a golden throne,
And sent word to the people, they say.
The Argyn and Kyrgyz gathered
And Prince Manas, the bloodstained warrior,
They raised as khan, they say.
He became lord of Talas;
They gave their unity to Manas.
Kengdeme, Keng-Kol, and Talas!
Do not belittle wolf-maned Manas.
From Alty-Shaar and Kokand,
Greathearted Manas then
Took tribute from those lands.
No foe remained to answer him back,
No claimant remained to plead against him.
Wearing his marten cap with its matching dress,
He reclined at ease, they say.
He kept a royal court and was khan,
A man firmly established;
His clothing was fox and sable,
His dealings with God upright,
His words suited the people.
For the Argyn and the Kyrgyz
He was an iron fortress wall.
Tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol and Talas
He wisely made his home.
His resourcefulness became known:
“He has overcome Alöökö,” they said,
“The Black Chinese and the Manzhuu
He has utterly slaughtered,” they said.
To the great khan of Kakanchyn,
Karykan, the news became known.
Hearing the name of Manas,
Karykan was filled with sorrow.
He burst into a terrible rage,
And from his golden throne
He toppled down.
He heard the news from a governor.
Saying, “I would avenge my father,”
Alöökö's Kongurbay
From Karykan of Beijing
Stood asking for a command.
Alöökö's Kongurbay
Went before the khan
And raged furiously:
“I heard from those who came:
An arrogant Burut hero has arisen,
And my father Alöökö,
I hear, he has overcome.
He seized my father,
Dragged him along the road,
And tore him open for the great dogs.
Alöökö's ten thousand troops
He trampled underfoot.
He shattered his walled fortress,
Toppled his earthen ramparts,
And scattered everything.
He split his governor in two;
The remaining gold and countless coins
Among all his people
He distributed and gave away.
My khan father's guard,
Kanggürü, escaped and came.
'This is exactly what happened,'
He told me with the news.
Bereft of my khan father,
How can I remain alive?
Against the Burut—your father's grave!—
Against the people called Burut,
If I do not avenge my father,
May I sink away as though never born.
That Burut has gone mad;
Let me try locking horns with him!
Every day, they say, they extend farther,
The strides of that Manas.
Chasing them toward Alty-Shaar,
He utterly slaughtered, they say,
The men of my father Alöökö.
His tongue speaks the Burut language;
That bastard, that bloodthirsty one,
Is our enemy at heart.
He is no son who will leave us unassailed,
No slave who will leave us unfought.
He slaughtered and devoured the lord of the white dwelling;
Of all your great possessions
Not a speck remains.
This is my request—agree to it:
Of the Chinese people of forty khans,
Leave no champion behind;
Gather every one for me.
Take an expert judge beside you,
And all those champions
Make file past for inspection.
Set apart a vast force of heroes;
Against the Burut who has gone mad
Let me try locking horns.
Try sending me!”
When Kongurbay said this,
Like something pricked in a gland,
Karykan leaped up.
Such was the nature of Karykan:
He was a most holy seer;
Suffering six months away
He could see and know this instant—
Such was his gift of knowledge.
An exalted sovereign, but not God,
Nor was he devoid of divine power.
To call him an infidel would not suffice;
Who Karykan truly was
Remains beyond our sight to this day.
The throne he sat on was a golden throne;
Upon that golden throne,
Addressing Kongurbay,
Karykan spoke in a booming voice:
“If you go against Manas, you will die.
The Chinese people of forty khans—
How will you return and see them?
Manas is no ordinary hero,
No lion a mortal may assail.
To slaughter when you take a fancy,
He is no Chinese people.
Do not ask about Manas:
Many years ago he became known;
His prowess is recorded with me,
Inscribed in the great register.
Written through unseen powers,
